clue.text: Note added to unusual tune for dance

indicators.note: an unusual tune is one not in its usual form, so its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the third note of the sol-fa scale
placement only: the note comes first and the rest is added after it
the four letters of TUNE rearranged

explanation.surface: A composer slips an extra note into an odd melody to make it danceable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' here is a sol-fa syllable (do, re, mi), not a written message.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain case of genus and species: the answer names one particular stately court dance in triple time.

clue.text: Area embracing state's belief system

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in your arms, so the area wraps round what follows

blocks.note: LI is the international code for the state of Liechtenstein

explanation.surface: A region that takes in a whole nation's creed.
explanation.walkthrough: LI for a state is unusual: it is Liechtenstein's country code, and even solvers at the time found it doubtful. The 's reads as 'state is', joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a faith is an organised system of belief and worship.

clue.text: Unkind people decapitated animals

indicators.note: to decapitate is to cut off the head, so the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: the first letter, R, comes off

explanation.surface: Cruel people cutting the heads off animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decapitated' reads as a grisly verb about the animals, but it acts on the word for unkind people.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the answer is one kind of animal, a river-dwelling mammal.

clue.text: Pope and priest working on disagreement

blocks.note: P is an abbreviation for priest
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: The Pope and one of his priests at work on settling a dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pope and priest' reads as two people, but only the Pope is the definition; 'and' joins it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the Pontiff is a formal title of the Pope, from the Latin for high priest.

clue.text: Drama series set in computerless IT company!

indicators.note: a show is set in a place, and here the letters are literally set inside the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of computerless, all of IT and the start of company

explanation.surface: A TV show about an IT firm that has no computers, which is its whole comic premise.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark hints at the joke: an IT company with no computers is exactly the absurd premise of a TV comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose definition: the answer is a situation comedy, a series of comic episodes, and 'drama' stretches to cover it.

clue.text: Adolescent going to Post Office for illicit liquor

blocks.note: placement only: the adolescent goes after the Post Office

explanation.surface: An underage youth sent to the post office to buy bootleg drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue order is reversed: the adolescent is named first but goes second, because it is 'going to' the Post Office.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain description: the answer is Irish moonshine, traditionally distilled illegally from potatoes.

clue.text: Fizzy gin and it does lead to organic decomposition

indicators.note: fizzy things bubble and churn, so the letters are stirred up

explanation.surface: A fizzy gin and Italian vermouth that upsets the stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: The italic 'it' is Italian vermouth, as in the cocktail gin and it; 'does' belongs to the fodder, not the grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic-leaning description: the body breaking food down chemically is a kind of organic decomposition.

clue.text: Storyline involving international aviator

indicators.note: a storyline involving something takes it in, so it holds the letter inside

explanation.surface: A plot about a globe-trotting flyer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'International aviator' reads as one phrase, but 'international' belongs to the wordplay and the aviator stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone who flies an aircraft.

clue.text: Setter's into dirty books to get first of six basic principles

indicators.note: the setter goes into the dirty word, so sits inside it
only the first letter of six is taken

blocks.note: 'setter is' said by the setter: I am

explanation.surface: The setter confesses to a taste for smutty books.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords the setter is 'I' or 'me', so 'setter's' means I'm. 'Dirty books' tempts as one idea, but books is its own piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the first elements of a subject that everything else builds on.

clue.text: Fastener made by special workers on ship

blocks.note: the people who work a vessel

explanation.surface: A bolt produced by a specialist team aboard a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Special workers' tempts as one phrase, but 'special' is a single letter and 'workers on ship' is one idea.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a threaded pin that holds things together is one type of fastener.

clue.text: Boy standing to welcome Hungary's first writer

indicators.note: in a down clue a word that stands up reads from bottom to top
to welcome someone is to take them in, so the boy holds the letter
only the first letter of Hungary is wanted

blocks.note: a boy is a lad, turned upward

explanation.surface: A boy on his feet greeting the first arrival from Hungary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standing' only works as a reversal in a down clue, where it sets the word on end.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Roald Dahl, author of Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, is a writer.

clue.text: Series of steps looks hard to an audience

indicators.note: an audience hears rather than reads, so what counts is the sound

blocks.note: to look hard is to stare

explanation.surface: A flight of steps glowering at a crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Looks hard' is a verb phrase and the definition a noun; only the sound carries across from one to the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a flight of steps between floors.

clue.text: Piece in newspaper covering Steptoe & Son?

indicators.note: a paper covering a story wraps round it, so the letters sit outside

blocks.note: the two title characters collected junk for a living

explanation.surface: A newspaper article about the old TV comedy Steptoe and Son.
explanation.walkthrough: Steptoe and Son was a British sitcom about a father and son who were rag-and-bone men, collecting junk from a horse-drawn cart; the question mark flags them as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a broken-off bit of something, with 'piece' also teasing a newspaper piece.

clue.text: Woman in short uniform

indicators.note: a word that is short falls short of its full length, losing its last letter

blocks.note: the last letter, N, is cut

explanation.surface: A woman wearing a skimpy uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform' looks like clothing but is the adjective meaning consistent.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the first woman in Genesis, and a woman's name.

clue.text: See 16
Terrible film about Newgate's first jailer

indicators.note: the film goes about, meaning around, the letter
only the first letter of Newgate is wanted

blocks.note: a flop at the box office is called a turkey

explanation.surface: A dreadful movie about the first warder at Newgate.
explanation.walkthrough: Newgate was a notorious London prison, which makes the jailer at home in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned synonym: the jailer is the one who turns the key in the cell door.

clue.text: List drug written up as class A

indicators.note: in a down answer, writing a word up means it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: a ship that lists leans over to one side
the drug is pot, cannabis, turned upward

explanation.surface: A drug listed on the record as a Class A substance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Class A' suggests the British drugs classification, but here it means first-rate. The answer continues at 15 down.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: excellent, of the very highest class.

clue.text: Sound of dry grass

indicators.note: the sound of a word, not its spelling, is wanted

explanation.surface: The rustle of parched grass in a field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dry grass' reads as hay, but 'dry' is the wordplay: wry, as in dry wit.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a cereal crop, and cereals are botanically grasses.

clue.text: Starts to eat dry and mouldy cheese

indicators.note: the starts of the words are their first letters

blocks.note: first letters of the four words

explanation.surface: Someone tucking into a stale, mouldy lump of cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is almost literal: the four words really do describe eating old cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a mild Dutch cheese sold in red wax.

clue.text: Snap shut?

blocks.note: a photograph taken at very short range
to shut a shop or a gap

explanation.walkthrough: 'Snap shut' reads as one action, but it splits: a snap is a photo, and 'shut' is a separate verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a photograph framed tightly on its subject, and the phrasal verb meaning to shut.

clue.text: Vet with ideas about drug

indicators.note: letters thrown about are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A veterinarian with thoughts on which medicine to use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vet' tempts as a verb meaning check, but it is just three letters of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a calming medicine is one kind of drug.

clue.text: Lecturer tucked into hot cake

indicators.note: something tucked into another thing sits inside it

explanation.surface: An academic eating a warm cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot cake' wants to be read together, but 'hot' is slang for stolen and the cake alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a German fruit loaf eaten at Christmas is one kind of cake.

clue.text: Graph in Chapter 1 redrawn

indicators.note: something redrawn is drawn again in a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: 1 is the Roman I; anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: A chart in a book's opening chapter that has been drawn again.
explanation.walkthrough: The digit 1 stands for the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a circle cut into slices is one kind of graph.

clue.text: Six surrounding American in pub to no avail

indicators.note: the six surrounds the American, sitting on both sides of it
the result goes in the pub, so sits inside it

explanation.surface: Six drinkers crowding round an American in a pub, getting nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: There are two containers, one nested inside the other: the inner pair is built first and then placed in the pub.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: an effort made without success was made to no avail.

clue.text: Worry about Tory leader joining large organisation restricting free trade

indicators.note: worry goes about, meaning around, the letter
the leader of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Concern that the Conservative Party leader is joining a big anti-competitive group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tory leader' tempts a real politician's name, but only the first letter is wanted. Tory is the nickname of the British Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a group of firms that collude to fix prices and shut out competition.

clue.text: Doctor taking drug to poor lad in madhouse

indicators.note: the doctor takes the rest in, holding it inside
a poor lad is in a bad way, so his letters are in bad order

explanation.surface: A doctor giving medicine to a sad boy in an asylum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is not an anagram indicator here but a degree abbreviation, and it takes in both the drug and the shuffled boy.
explanation.definitionFit: An eponym: London's Bethlem asylum was nicknamed Bedlam, so the word came to mean a madhouse or uproar.

clue.text: Drive away with panini filling during celebration

indicators.note: the filling of a sandwich is its middle
something that happens during a party is inside it

blocks.note: the middle two letters of the six

explanation.surface: Heading off with a stuffed sandwich from a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Filling' sounds like a sandwich filling, and that is exactly the joke: it takes the centre of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to send someone away and forbid their return.

clue.text: Publicity about animal on ship

indicators.note: the publicity goes about, meaning around, the animal

explanation.surface: An advert for an animal carried by sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Animal' is vague on purpose; a short one like a boar fits the four-letter gap left by the publicity.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the adverb for being on a vessel, as in 'all aboard'.

clue.text: Endless destitution is plain for all to see

indicators.note: without ends: both the first and last letters go

blocks.note: P and Y come off the two ends

explanation.surface: Grinding poverty that is obvious to everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' strips both ends, not just the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: done openly, not hidden.

clue.text: Aircraft got diverted around Zimbabwean leader's la-la land

indicators.note: a diverted flight changes course, so the letters change order
the shuffled letters go around the Z
the leader of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A plane rerouted around a dictator's fantasy world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Zimbabwean leader' suggests Mugabe, but only the letter Z is wanted. Planet Zog is British slang for an imaginary place where out-of-touch people live.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang equivalent: both phrases name an imaginary place for someone out of touch with reality.

clue.text: Attach an inner layer to navy fabric

blocks.note: to put a lining in a coat

explanation.surface: A tailor putting a lining into a navy-blue cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Navy' looks like a colour of fabric but is just a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: cloth woven from flax is one kind of fabric.

clue.text: Soldier on exercise to reverse changes

indicators.note: the word undergoes changes, so its letters move

explanation.surface: A soldier on a drill being told to turn back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soldier' looks like a noun but is the verb in 'soldier on'; 'reverse' is fodder, not a reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to soldier on is to keep going despite difficulty.
